title: Child marriage complaints to 999 halve since 2023, data show
excerpt: Calls to 999 about child marriage fell from 6,499 in 2023 to 3,045 in 2025, Prothom Alo reported. NGOs say the practice has not declined.

image.alt: The front of the main building of Domrakandi High School in rural Bangladesh
image.credit: File photo: Riajul islam riaj / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

content:
DHAKA, 28 November 2026: Fewer child marriages are being reported and stopped in Bangladesh, but people who work on the issue say this does not mean the practice is declining, Prothom Alo reported on Friday (27 November), the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage. The day falls during the 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence.

Department of Women Affairs figures cited by the newspaper show that officials prevented 1,846 child marriages in 2023, 1,474 in 2024 and 968 in 2025, a fall of 48% in two years, and 479 from January to June 2026. Calls to the National Emergency Service 999 about child marriage fell from 6,499 in 2023 to 4,109 in 2024 and 3,045 in 2025. There were 2,548 calls from January to August 2026, about 11 a day against 18 a day in 2023. Prothom Alo put the overall fall at "as much as 40%"; Devlens has used the published department and 999 figures.

Soma Dutta, programme manager at Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF), told Prothom Alo that field experience showed child marriage had not fallen. Kaniz Sultana, a project officer at the Village Education Resource Centre (VERC) in Rangabali, Patuakhali, said many families marry girls off in secret, knowing it is an offence. Laila Khondkar, convenor of the group Shishurai Shob, who visited chars in Gaibandha and Sirajganj in July, said: "Everyone is treating child marriage as normal and giving up, believing that it cannot be eliminated. As a result, not all cases are being reported." She said groups promoting child marriage had appeared on social media.

Catherine Breen Kamkong, Representative of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) in Bangladesh, said there is no integrated database of government services, so a fall at one office does not show an overall fall. There is no follow-up after a marriage is stopped, she said, so families often marry the girl elsewhere, and people who complain fear exposure. Kamkong again called for Section 19 of the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, which allows a marriage under 18 with a court order and parental consent, to be amended.

Women and Children Affairs Minister A Z M Zahid Hossain told Prothom Alo on 3 November that the government would take effective measures and seek local people's views.

Why it matters

Marriages stopped are often counted as programme results, so falling reports can hide a growing problem. UNFPA said on Friday that marriage among girls aged 15-19 has risen to 39% (see Devlens' report), and the MICS 2025 district atlas shows where rates are highest. For NGOs running adolescent clubs and community reporting, the gaps are follow-up after a marriage is stopped and protection for those who report.

What to watch

  • Department of Women Affairs prevention figures for July to December 2026.
  • Any move to amend Section 19, and the consultations the minister promised.
  • Begum Rokeya Day on 9 December and the close of the 16 Days campaign on 10 December (see the Events page).
